report:
## Research Summary

The claim is well-supported by high-quality randomized controlled trial evidence.

**Key evidence: The MAP.3 (NCIC CTG MAP.3) trial**
This was a large, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial of 4,560 postmenopausal women at moderately increased risk of breast cancer (based on age, Gail risk score, prior atypical hyperplasia/DCIS, etc.). Participants received either exemestane (25 mg/day) or placebo. Results, presented at ASCO 2011 and published in the *New England Journal of Medicine*, showed exemestane reduced the incidence of invasive breast cancer by 65% compared with placebo after a median follow-up of 35 months, with annual incidence of 0.19% vs. 0.55% in the placebo group ([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507); [cancer.gov](https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/research/exemestane-reduces-risk)). Adverse events were generally similar between groups, though exemestane caused known aromatase-inhibitor-related side effects such as menopausal symptoms and mild negative effects on quality of life and bone density were noted in substudies ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/PMC3354700](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3354700/)).

**Comparison with other agents**
Reviews note that aromatase inhibitors like exemestane produced a greater relative risk reduction than SERMs (tamoxifen ~49% reduction, raloxifene lower efficacy), while causing fewer serious side effects such as thromboembolism and endometrial cancer, though they raise concerns about bone loss ([researchgate.net/Tamoxifen_vs_Raloxifene_vs_Exemestane](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/255977089_Tamoxifen_vs_Raloxifene_vs_Exemestane_for_Chemoprevention)).

**Caveats**
Follow-up in MAP.3 was relatively short (median ~35 months), and long-term data on overall survival, fractures, and durability of benefit remain limited, though later analyses reaffirm the reduction with longer follow up.

**Conclusion:** The claim is accurate and supported by solid RCT evidence, though benefits should be weighed against menopausal and bone-related side effects.
